tldr: This is a pattern across independent projects, not one event. It opened with vLLM's Kinference, an open-source control plane for serving vLLM on Kubernetes, plus a third-party benchmark of it against plain Kubernetes, then moved to an InfoQ podcast on llm-d.
whats_new: Distributed inference work has moved from datacenter clusters to local hardware: an arXiv paper (Superfluid) on a local server shared by several agents, then a Show HN project (Shard) that splits inference across multiple computers.
why_it_matters: Multi-node serving is splitting into two tracks: Kubernetes control planes that add tenant rate limits and cost tracking around vLLM, and local setups that pool your own machines to keep data private and avoid per-token cost.

beats.headline: vLLM ships Kinference, a Kubernetes control plane, and a benchmark follows
beats.summary: Token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, and load balancing for vLLM, then Buoyant's comparison against plain Kubernetes.

beats.headline: InfoQ podcast covers llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes
Research and hobby projects take distributed inference off the cluster
beats.summary: Superfluid targets one device shared by several agents; Shard spreads a model across several computers.

open_questions: Does Buoyant's benchmark show Kinference beating plain Kubernetes on latency or throughput, and under what load?
Will Kinference and llm-d converge, or stay competing control planes for vLLM on Kubernetes?
Does Superfluid release code, and how does it schedule several agents on one local model?
What network bandwidth does Shard need before splitting a model across machines beats running it on one?
take_for_builders: If you run vLLM on Kubernetes and hand-roll per-tenant rate limits or cost tracking, check Kinference and llm-d before building more, and read the benchmark's setup before trusting its numbers.
